extracted.intended_audience: users of PARI/GP (primarily number theorists and computational mathematicians who program with the PARI library or the gp calculator)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for installing, configuring, programming in, and using the PARI/GP system (gp calculator and libpari), with performance and correctness recommendations for mathematical computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiprecision kernel choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The PARI multiprecision kernel comes in three non exclusive flavors: (1) ANSI C (portable), (2) inlined assembler for time-critical parts on specific architectures, and (3) a GMP-backed kernel (uses the GNU MP library).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ANSI C kernel for portability to any 32 or 64-bit machine. Use the assembler kernels for performance on supported architectures (ix86, Sparc variants, DEC Alpha, Itanium, PowerPC, HPPA). Enable the GMP kernel when GMP is present for much better performance on large operands (≈100 decimal digits or more). See Appendix A for setup and supported compilers (gcc recommended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portability principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the ANSI C kernel when portability across many systems is required: 'A first version is written entirely in ANSI C... and should be portable without trouble to any 32 or 64-bit computer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you expect to run PARI on many different machines or under varying compilers/environments, avoid relying on architecture-specific assembler kernels; instead use the ANSI C or GMP kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modes of PARI appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI is used in three different ways: (1) as a library libpari callable from C/C++, (2) as the gp programmable calculator (GP language), and (3) gp2c which translates GP code to C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose libpari for embedding or maximal efficiency in larger applications; use gp for interactive exploration and quick scripts; use gp2c to compile frequently-run GP scripts (typical speedup 3–10x) and to obtain editable/generated C code for further optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read tutorial and reference first
rubrics_metrics.description: A tutorial (tuto rial.dvi) is provided and should be read first; refcard gives a quick overview and Chapter 3 contains complete function descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the tutorial to learn idiomatic GP usage before diving into the full manual. Use the refcard for quick lookup and Chapter 3 for details on individual functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bug reporting procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Bugs are submitted online to the Bug Tracking System available from PARI’s home page or directly at http://pari.math.u-bordeaux.fr/Bugs/.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the instructions on the Bugs page when reporting issues (include version, kernel, system info as prompted).

rubrics_metrics.name: PARI philosophy on operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations and functions should, firstly, give as exact a result as possible, and secondly, be permitted if they make any kind of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and use functions so they return exact results for exact inputs and sensible results for mixed/edge inputs; this principle guides automatic coercions and behaviour across types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact vs inexact object handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Types t_REAL, t_PADIC and t_SER are imprecise; an object is inexact if any node in its tree has an imprecise type. Exact operations on exact objects yield exact objects; operations involving inexact objects produce results 'as precise as possible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on exact arithmetic (integers, rationals, polmods, etc.) when exactness is required. When mixing exact and inexact types, be aware that result precision depends on operand precisions, values, and cancellations (e.g., x+y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default precision usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The default precision is only used to convert exact types to inexact ones; it is not a general control of final precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume default precision guarantees result precision; when converting exact to inexact types, be explicit about required precision, and monitor accuracy-sensitive computations carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: When operations involve objects of different accuracies, some digits will be disregarded; accuracy of real/inexact results depends on operands' precisions, magnitudes, and cancellations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: e.g., small numbers < machine epsilon may be treated as exact zeros; examples: 0.E-28 + 1.E-100 yields 0.E-28. Understand how exponents and mantissas determine equivalence to zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive automatic mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI operations are permissive: applying a scalar function to a vector or matrix is interpreted componentwise; when objects of different types are combined, they are mapped to a suitable ring for the computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permissiveness is convenient (e.g., exp(vector) applies exp to each element) but be aware of implicit coercions and ring changes (e.g., mixing Mod(.,15) and Mod(.,10) may map computations into Z/5Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix-function ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: An ambiguity arises with square matrices: PARI assumes componentwise evaluation for functions on square matrices, so standard matrix functions (like matrix exponential) need special implementations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need a true matrix exponential or other non-componentwise matrix operation, implement or call a specific matrix-aware routine rather than relying on the scalar-function behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer exact division where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Division is, as far as possible, an exact operation: 4 divided by 3 gives (4/3) (a rational), not a floating point approximation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use integer/rational division for exact arithmetic; use 1./3 or 0.+1/3 to force real (floating point) division when a floating result is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency: avoid overuse of reduction-heavy types
rubrics_metrics.description: Types provided for convenience (t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, t_PADIC, t_POLMOD, t_RFRAC) always perform reductions after elementary operations and are thus not the most efficient for heavy computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large computations prefer working with integers and delaying reductions, use libpari for lower-level efficient operations, or employ homomorphic imaging/modular schemes. Example: computing polynomial convolutions is faster if you avoid per-operation reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular arithmetic for modular needs
rubrics_metrics.description: If only modular information is required, it is more efficient to work directly with t_INTMODs than to compute full rational or integer results and reduce afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sum(i=1,10^5,Mod(1/i,p)) is far faster than computing sum of rationals then reducing mod p. Prefer Mod(a,b) for Z/bZ computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type recursion constraints and sensible usage
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI types are recursive; components of recursive types can themselves be arbitrary types, but creating pathological recursive objects (e.g., 'complex numbers of complex numbers') is permitted in library mode but typically yields nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructs that create nested incompatible recursions. When in gp calculator mode, some pathological recursive types are disallowed; in library mode they are allowed but likely produce meaningless results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on integer/real sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Integers and real numbers are arbitrary-length but subject to practical internal limits (e.g., on 32-bit machines integers must have absolute value < 2^536870815 roughly). Real precision also has maximum bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of system-dependent hard limits on representable sizes/precisions; consult the manual for exact bounds and plan algorithms accordingly to avoid overflow or impractically large objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and meaning of zero for inexact types
rubrics_metrics.description: For inexact types (p-adics, power series, reals) zeros carry exponents: p-adic or X-adic zero is O(p^e) or O(X^e); real zeros are O(2^e) and are printed in e-format (0.Exx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reasoning about equality with zero, consider the exponent/precision; two real zeros with different exponents are treated equal, but small numbers below exponent thresholds may be treated as zero in computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: GP input and evaluation model
rubrics_metrics.description: GP is an interpreted language whose input is byte-compiled to bytecode and then evaluated; expressions always have values; sequences of expressions (separated by ;) return the value of the last expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand evaluation order, how semicolons affect printing but not storage in history, and that sequences discard intermediate values unless assigned. Use semicolon to suppress printing for large results but assign to variables if you need them later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command-line startup and defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: Start gp with 'gp [-D key=val ] [files]'; preferences (gprc) are read on startup and defaults can be changed on the command line, interactively, or in the preferences file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize defaults via -D options or gprc; if extended help or readline is missing in the banner, check installation (GMP kernel mention) with the installer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Help system usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use '?' for the top-level help menu; '?n' to list commands in category n; '?functionname' for a short explanation; '??' for complete description; '???' to search functions relevant to a query; '?\' for metacommands; '? . ' for member functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the multi-? levels to get progressively more detailed help. If extended help is available, ?? and ??? are especially useful for documentation and searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: GP metacommands and metacontrol
rubrics_metrics.description: Commands beginning with '\' or '?' are metacommands (not computing commands) to change gp internal state, defaults, or perform simple shortcuts and shortcuts/keyboard shortcuts are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn metacommands (see Section 2.13) to manage defaults, timers, and session behaviour efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line editing and multiline input rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Line editing (readline) provides history and completion. To continue lines use backslash at end of line, use a newline after '=' when assigning, or use braces { } for multi-line blocks (braces do not nest and newlines inside are concatenated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not split identifiers across concatenated lines inside braces; insert semicolons or commas at logical breakpoints. Use backslash for simple continuations and braces for multi-line code blocks (e.g., function bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: History behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: GP stores results in a history array (%1, %2, ...) up to a default size of 5000 (queue behaviour). Suppressed printing still stores the result. Use %# to recover time used to compute history entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on absolute history indices for long sessions (older entries are dropped). Adjust histsize if necessary; assign important results to named variables instead of relying solely on %n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrupt and quitting behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing Ctrl-C interrupts the current computation and reports where and how long it was running; 'quit' ends the gp session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Ctrl-C to safely abort long computations and inspect where the runtime was; use 'quit' to end sessions cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Member functions to inspect complex types
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types provide member functions to access internal data; e.g., for t_INTMOD x.mod returns the modulus, and for finite field elements g.pol, g.p, g.f, g.mod provide polynomial representation, characteristic, field dimension, and minimal polynomial respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provided member functions to inspect and manipulate compound objects instead of trying to deconstruct internal representations manually.

rubrics_metrics.name: I/O and print suppression conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ending a gp expression with ';' suppresses printing of the result though it is still computed and stored; print() is a procedure that produces side-effects and returns a void object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ';' to avoid printing large results; assign results to variables when you wish to keep them. Remember procedure returns may be the special void which evaluates to 0 in numeric contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real number input semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Real numbers are input with a decimal point; trailing zeros affect internal precision; scientific notation is accepted; 0.E n yields a real zero of exponent n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When entering constants, include trailing digits if you need specific precision. Use scientific form appropriately to capture desired exponent/precision for zeros and tiny numbers.
